title: Newton’s Gravity
objective: After this level you can explain how one law of gravity covers falling apples, orbiting moons and planets.
summary: Newton’s universal gravitation (1687) showed one force governs falling objects, the Moon and the planets, explaining Kepler’s laws.

cards.headline: The force that drops an apple also holds the Moon in the sky.
cards.body: Kepler described how the planets move. Newton explained why, and the answer was the same thing that pulls your toast to the kitchen floor.

cards.headline: One law for everything
cards.body: In 1687 Isaac Newton published his law of universal gravitation. Every object pulls on every other. The pull grows with their masses and weakens with the square of the distance: twice as far, a quarter of the pull. You'd feel the difference on the Moon, where surface gravity is only about one-sixth of Earth's, so you would weigh about one-sixth as much. Great news for your high jump.
cards.callout: Twice as far → ¼ the pull

cards.headline: Heaven and Earth, united
cards.body: Here's the big leap. The gravity that makes an apple fall on Earth is the same force that keeps the Moon in orbit and the planets circling the Sun. One force, from your kitchen to the edge of the solar system. It also explained why Kepler's laws work, turning a description into an explanation. It even reaches the beach: the Moon's gravity pulling on the oceans is what raises the tides (Level 17).

mascot.line: If you remember one thing from this level: the gravity in your kitchen is the gravity that steers the planets.

cards.headline: Gravity: understood
learned: Every object pulls on every other
Double the distance → a quarter of the pull

questions.prompt: What did Newton show about gravity?

options.label: Gravity only works near the surface of Earth
options.rationale: His key insight was that it works everywhere.

options.label: One force makes apples fall and holds the Moon in orbit
It pushes planets away from the Sun
It only pulls on large, heavy objects like planets
options.rationale: Every object pulls on every other.

questions.explanation: Newton’s universal gravitation: one force explains falling objects on Earth and the motions of the Moon and planets.

questions.prompt: If you doubled the distance between two objects, what would happen to their gravitational pull?

options.label: It would drop to a quarter

questions.explanation: Gravity weakens with the square of the distance: twice as far means 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 of the pull.

questions.prompt: From Level 17: what connects Newton’s law to the ocean tides?

options.label: The Moon’s gravity pulls on Earth’s oceans
Tides come from Earth’s orbit around the Sun
options.rationale: Tides are mainly the Moon’s pull.

options.label: Newton’s law says water isn’t affected by gravity
options.rationale: Gravity pulls on everything, including water.

options.label: Tides happen only at the equator

questions.explanation: Newton’s gravity acts between all masses. The Moon’s pull on the oceans creates the tidal bulges.
